page.title: Odor Predictor | Simon Cui
hero.title: Predicting smell from molecular structure
hero.intro: What a molecule smells like is largely decided by its structure: which atoms it contains and how they are connected. This project trains an AI model, a graph neural network, to read a molecule's structure and predict the words flavorists would use to describe its smell, such as fruity, buttery or roasted. Tools like this can help flavor developers screen candidate molecules on a computer before going into the lab.

method.title: How it works
flow.1.title: Molecule
flow.2.title: Graph
flow.2.sub: atoms are nodes, bonds are edges
flow.3.title: Graph neural network
flow.3.sub: atoms pass information to their neighbors, 3 rounds
flow.4.title: Odor descriptors
flow.4.sub: a probability for each of 138 words
method.data: Data. 4,886 molecules with expert odor descriptions from two flavor and fragrance databases (The Good Scents Company and Leffingwell), merged and cleaned by the OpenPOM project. Each molecule has about 5 of 138 possible descriptors.
method.model: Model. Each atom starts with a few simple properties: element, number of neighbors and hydrogens, charge, aromaticity and whether it is in a ring. In each round every atom collects information from the atoms bonded to it. The result is pooled into one summary of the whole molecule and turned into 138 probabilities. The model has about 140,000 parameters, small enough to run in a web browser.
method.eval: Fair testing. Molecules with rings were split into training (80%), validation (10%) and test (10%) sets by ring scaffold, so the test set contains ring systems the model never saw. This is harder, and more honest, than a purely random split.
results.title: How well does it work?
results.intro: Performance is measured with AUROC. Take one molecule that has a descriptor and one that does not: AUROC is the chance that the model gives the first one a higher score. 0.5 is random guessing and 1.0 is perfect. The numbers below are averaged over all 138 descriptors on the 488 test molecules.
results.seed_note: Graph neural network: scores of the model deployed on this page. Across 3 training runs with different random seeds, the overall score was {mean} (standard deviation {std}). The baselines describe each molecule by a list of the small structural fragments it contains (a Morgan fingerprint) and use standard machine learning methods.
results.takeaway: The graph neural network beats both conventional baselines by about 0.02 AUROC. The gain is modest but consistent across random seeds and across most descriptors. Molecules with ring systems not seen during training are clearly harder (about 0.80).
results.label_note: Only descriptors with at least 10 positive molecules in the test set are listed.
limits.title: Limitations
limits.4: Predictions for ring systems unlike anything in the training data are noticeably weaker (AUROC about 0.80).
limits.6: Not for safety decisions. It says nothing about toxicity, allergenicity or regulatory status.
